blocks.p: Rei found the ninth seat the way sailors find weather. He looked for the place where the city bent around it.

Higuchi's note gave no address, because there was no address to give. Gin's file said the only safe way to reach the Hunger holder was through the Grid's emergency network, and that night Rei had nobody in the Grid to ask. So he used what Higuchi had given him instead. Not an address but a habit. A route that was never the same route twice. And one line in Higuchi's cramped handwriting.
He eats so he does not have to stop, and he moves so the appetite cannot find the door.

So Rei took the Keihin-Tōhoku line south to Ueno after dark. The sky-blue train was packed with people heading into the city for the evening. A group of university boys passed round a bag of crisps. A woman in a summer kimono stood by the door, holding a paper fan, her hair pinned up with a comb shaped like a goldfish. At Ueno the doors opened onto heat, noise and the smell of food.

It was the second week of Obon. The air around the station was thick with grilling fat, incense and the sweet burnt smell of taiyaki, little fish-shaped cakes filled with bean paste, cooked in iron moulds at street stalls. Lanterns swung over the food stalls. Under the railway the crowds moved in slow, warm currents, and the sound of trains passing overhead came down through the steel like thunder. Rei passed ramen counters that stayed open all night, and conveyor-belt sushi places still lit up at one in the morning. He was not looking for a face. He was looking for a kind of movement. Somewhere between the station and the park he began to feel it, the way he had felt the cold on the stairwell. An inward pull. A low, steady note under the noise of the festival.
More.

It was not Rei's own wanting. It was a wanting that belonged to nothing in particular. It never became a wish for food or drink or company. It was simply appetite with the object rubbed off, reaching into Rei and feeling around in his own emptiness for something to hold.
The man was at a standing counter eating gyoza, little fried dumplings, and he had already half turned to leave before the plate was finished.

He was in his late thirties and looked older. Tall and thin, all long arms and legs, his hair grown out and not recently cut. He was neat, but it was a neatness that had gone threadbare at the cuffs. He wore a jacket with too many pockets and carried a bag he could pick up in one movement. He moved like a man who owned only what he could carry, and who had learned to eat fast and walk faster.

He did not sit. Rei would come to understand that he had not properly sat down in three years. The stools and benches and chairs of the city were all, in a small way, his enemies. The one piece of furniture he truly feared was a bed.

He noticed Rei the moment the appetite in the air touched Rei and Rei touched it back. He felt his own register find a foothold in a stranger. His eyes went to Rei with the tired, practised caution of a man who has been hunted by things far quieter than this boy.

"You feel it," he said around the last dumpling, already paying, already moving. "Then walk while you talk. If I stand here much longer it learns this counter. I like this counter. I'd rather not have to give it up."
So they walked.

They passed a conveyor-belt sushi bar, where little plates went round and round on a belt under a lit counter. A young salaryman sat at the end of it, his tie loosened, a tower of empty plates by his elbow. He was reaching for another plate before he had finished chewing. His face had the slack, faraway look of a man who is not eating because he is hungry. He was eating because he could not think what else to do with his hands.
As Satoru walked past the window, the man's hand stopped halfway to the belt. He blinked. He looked at the plates beside him as if he were seeing them for the first time, and set his chopsticks down.

"That's it," Satoru said, without looking back. "That's the whole job. The appetite gets into a man and he doesn't know why he's eating. I walk past and take the empty off him, and he goes home and thinks he's had enough. Fifty of those a night. A hundred, in a bad week." He did not slow down. "If I'd stopped at the counter beside him, I'd have given it to him instead. The empty goes where the holder is. That's why the holder can't be anywhere for long."

He set a pace that was not quite a hurry and never once slowed. He wove through the festival crowds, past families coming back from the temple with their lanterns, past the long warm tables of the night markets. As he moved, the wanting moved with him, half a step behind. It was like a thing on a leash, and he stayed just ahead of it by never, ever stopping.
"Inoue Satoru," he said, once they were clear of the counter and the appetite had let go of it. "Ninth of the Thirteen. I carry Hunger."
He said it the way another man might say he had a bad heart. A fact about the body. Heavy, permanent, not up for discussion.
"And before you ask the thing everyone asks. No. I cannot just put it down for one night and sleep. That is exactly the thing I cannot do. That is the whole job."

He explained it as they walked from Ueno toward Okachimachi, the next station down the line. On this stretch the railway runs high on brick arches, and the spaces under the arches are packed with tiny shops and bars. The late izakaya were still going, the small cheap pubs where people sit close together over beer and grilled skewers. Smoke from the grills drifted out under the red lanterns, and men in shirtsleeves laughed too loudly at plastic tables on the pavement. Satoru explained it walking, always walking, because explaining it standing still would have shown the problem.

"A holder doesn't satisfy the register," he said. "You can't. Hunger isn't a wanting that gets a thing and stops. It's the wanting underneath all the wantings. The empty that's there before there's anything to fill it. My job isn't to feed it. My job is to keep it from finding out where it lives."

His jacket pockets bulged. Rei saw what was in them when Satoru reached into one. Wrapped sweets, rice crackers, a paper twist of roasted chestnuts. He ate the way other men smoke, without noticing, to keep his hands and mouth busy so the rest of him would not slow down.

"Don't look at me like that," Satoru said. "I'm not hungry. I'm never hungry. It isn't my hunger." He offered Rei a chestnut. Rei took it. It was still warm, and it tasted of nothing at all, as if the empty walking beside them had eaten the taste out of it first.
He bought a skewer of grilled chicken from a stall without breaking stride, ate it in four bites and dropped the stick into a bin he had clearly used before.

"Every time I stop somewhere long enough, it learns the place. It writes the address down. And a Hunger seat with a fixed address starts pulling the empty toward it. Out of the people nearby. Out of the food, which stops being enough. Out of the holder, until the holder is the hungriest thing in the room and the room is starting to come apart. So I move. Three years now. The appetite doesn't get a door because I don't have one."

At the next crossing the lights turned red against them. Rei stopped at the kerb. Satoru did not. One moment he was beside Rei. The next he was on the far pavement, thirty metres away, waiting, with no gap in between where he had walked. Rei crossed on the green, and Satoru fell in beside him as if nothing had happened.

"Teleportation," Satoru said. "Short hops. The seat needs fast hands. Hunger doesn't flare in one place, it flares in fifty little places at once all over the city, and somebody has to be at each of them before it settles." He rubbed his eyes. "I try not to do it in front of people. It feels like cheating at walking."
"Gin's file said you were an emergency succession."

"The man before me died. Three years ago. The seat went empty, and they found me and put me in it in months. It's meant to take years. Years of preparation, years of being taught by the one before you." He shrugged. "I know where the gaps are. I'm managing them. The Axis knows too."

Walking that warm midnight beside a man who could not stop, Rei understood the plain, unglamorous truth of a seat. It was not a throne. It was a sentence. It was not power. It was a load a man built his whole life around, so that he would never drop it.

Satoru's tiredness had become part of his body. He slept in ninety-minute pieces on moving trains. He had not tasted a meal in years, because eating was upkeep and never pleasure. He had given up every fixed thing a life is made from. A home. A chair he liked. A person who knew which station to find him at. All of it, so that the empty he carried would never learn an address it could pull the world into.

"People think the hard part is the hunger," he said. "It isn't. The hard part is that I'd give anything to stop. Anything. And the one thing the register knows about me, the only handle it's got, is how badly I want to sit down."

And there it was. The crack. The same shape Rei had seen in two other failing seats. The human want that the impersonal register got its fingers into. The Fear holder had been afraid of failing. This one was starving for rest.

The domain was weather. It was nobody's fault. It was one of the true empties the world was built on, and somebody had to carry it. But the longing to set it down was his own. It was exactly the gap the appetite reached for. And he could not stop feeling it, because he was a tired man not yet forty who looked fifty, and he had not slept in a bed for longer than he could easily remember.

He glanced sideways at Rei as they walked, reading the pressed-down registers, the searching, the shaped thing. The others had looked at Rei with caution or with hope. Satoru looked at him with something worse. He recognised him.
"You've got an empty too," he said quietly. "Walled up. I can feel the door from here. How do you stand it not eating you?"
Rei asked him the question he asked all of them now. He had stopped believing in coincidence and started believing in a method.
"Has anyone been kind to you lately? Soft-voiced. Turned up around the time it got harder. Offered you something that felt like exactly what you needed, and left you a little worse than before."
Satoru stopped.
He really stopped, for the first time. One full second of stillness, and Rei could see what it cost him. The appetite lurched forward against its leash, and he made himself move again.

"There's a woman," he said. "Kitagawa-san. Runs a little guesthouse near Nippori. The old wooden kind. She found me. I don't know how. I don't have an address for anyone to find. She said she had a room with my name on it. No charge. A real bed. She said a man my age shouldn't have to sleep standing up. She was so kind about it I nearly cried, and I haven't done that in years."
He swallowed.

"I've been three times. I never stay. But each time it's harder to leave. And each time, for about a week after, the appetite is worse. I thought that was just wanting the bed I couldn't have. The contrast."
It was not the contrast. Rei knew this handwriting now. It was the patient kindness that hollowed out the chairs holding up the sky.

Someone had found the one thing a Hunger holder could not afford to want. A place to stop. They had wrapped it in a soft voice, a real bed and a room with his name on it. Every time he came, they let him taste the rest he had refused himself for three years. And every time, they let the appetite taste the address he had spent three years refusing to give it.

They were not trying to feed him. They were teaching the empty where its holder would live if he ever allowed himself to. They were drawing it toward one fixed door, one kind night at a time. In the end the seat would find an address, and the ninth domain would settle and start to pull. It would happen right beside a membrane that was already thin, in the one week of the year when the doors between here and the other side were propped open for the dead.

"I know what they're after," Satoru said, when Rei told him. He did not sound surprised. He sounded like a man hearing a diagnosis he had been avoiding. "We all feel it in the network. Somebody organised has been leaning on the seats for years. Not loose things. A campaign. It's coordinated from the very top of the scale, the Class S things that have their own institutions on the far side. And mine is the seat they want most." He walked faster. "They've been testing. Twice at the Shibuya crossing, two test events the CVD wrote up as crowd incidents. They keep two contact points in the underground mall at the Ikebukuro west exit. They don't want to take the thirteenth. They want it never to be filled, ever. A vacant thirteenth means the Axis is stretched across two jobs, and a stretched Axis makes mistakes. They've been living off its mistakes for three years. If they get mine as well..."
"Two empty seats," Rei said.

"Two empty seats, and the Axis tries to hold mine too and can't, because it's already holding Duty. Then it all starts sliding." He nodded north, toward Kita. "When Hunger goes, it won't go quietly. It'll go to the old works at Kita-Ōji first. The pre-war factories. There are suffering beings in those buildings nobody ever cleared. Hunger is what wakes them. That's where the first crossings would be."

"She asked me to come tonight," he said, and the appetite spiked as he said it, the way the fear had spiked when the stairwell holder named her visitor. "She said the room's made up. She said I looked so tired last time. She's not... I don't think she's pretending. That's the thing. I think she really does want to give a tired man a place to sleep. That's what makes it impossible to say no to."
He was walking faster now, as if he could outrun the offer itself.

"And I want to go. God help me, I want to go and lie down on a real bed and sleep eight hours and let it learn the address and let the whole thing settle and be someone else's problem. Because I am so tired, and three years is so long, and a bed is such a small thing to want."
He looked at Rei.
"So before I walk myself to Nippori like I do every time, tell me what you are. Because I think you might be the only person who could make it so I don't have to."
What Rei did was not the bed, and it was not the road.

He had walked enough of the night beside Satoru to see the whole trap. Satoru could not rest, because resting meant stopping. Stopping meant an address. And an address meant the seat would settle and pull. The guesthouse offered him stillness and poisoned it. The street offered him safety and never let him stop. They were the same sentence wearing two faces.
So Rei gave him the third thing, the one nobody had offered him in three years. He carried the movement for him.

blocks.cap: The whole city moving through the Obon night

blocks.p: It was Obon, and the whole city was on the move. Families were coming home from visiting the graves. Processions with lanterns wound through the streets. A slow river of people was heading down to the water for the tōrō nagashi, to set their paper lanterns floating on the current. Each lantern had a candle inside and a name written on its side, and the river would carry it, and the one it was for, back to the far shore.

Rei took Satoru down to the river, into the moving crowd. He walked on the outside, between Satoru and every place he might stop. He set the pace, so that Satoru did not have to. And for the length of the procession, inside the movement of ten thousand people walking the dead home, a man who had not sat down in three years closed his eyes and let himself be carried.

He did not sleep, exactly. But he rested, in a way he had forgotten was possible. He was moving without having to drive the movement himself, held inside a current bigger than his own exhaustion. The appetite found no door, because the whole street was moving, and there was no still place for it to write down.

Rei walked and kept walking. He took the empty into his own walled chest, where it could not reach all the way in. He stayed half a step ahead of Satoru, the way he had climbed half a step ahead of the fear. He was being hungry in the right place, on purpose, so that for one hour the man could run clean.

It was the worst kind of usefulness. Rei felt the old quiet voice start up under the noise of the festival. See, the wall is good, the empty can't eat you, why would you ever take it down. He kept that voice at the edge of the crowd with the rest of what he carried. He walked Satoru down to the water with his eyes closed and his face, for the first time, not braced against anything.
At the river's edge, lanterns were going out onto the black water by the hundred. Small boxes of orange light, released downstream toward the dead.
Satoru opened his eyes and watched them go.
"They don't stop either," he said softly. "That's the trick of it. They're not at rest. They're at peace because they're still moving."

Something in him had eased that no bed could have eased. Not the hunger. That was weather and would always be weather. It was the three-year cramp of a man who had believed his only choices were a chair that would kill him or a road that never ended.

Rei had not cured the ninth seat. He had shown its holder a way to be still inside movement. That was the one thing the soft-voiced woman's bed could never give him. Her stillness came with an address. Rei's came with a current.
"I didn't know it could be like this," Satoru said, watching the lights float away. "I thought stopping was the only way to rest. Nobody ever told me I could rest by being carried."

blocks.cap: The old wooden guesthouse near Nippori, its screens lit gold

blocks.p: They walked back up toward Nippori through the old streets, where the houses were low and wooden and the temples stood close together behind their walls. The crowds thinned. A cat watched them from the top of a wall. Kitagawa-san was waiting near the bottom of the guesthouse lane when they arrived.

blocks.cap: Kitagawa-san at the bottom of the guesthouse lane

blocks.p: She was exactly as Satoru had described her. A small, kind woman in late middle age, wearing an apron over a summer yukata. Behind her the guesthouse glowed warm, its paper screens lit gold. Rei did not doubt there was a real bed made up inside, with Satoru's name beside it.
She saw that he was not alone. And she saw, the way the soft-voiced ones always saw, that something tonight had not gone the way the method needed.

"Inoue-san," she said. Her voice was truly glad and truly worried, and the worry did its soft work of reaching for the want. "You look so tired. The room's ready. It's always ready. You don't have to keep doing this to yourself."

Rei watched him hear it. The rest. The room. The small mercy that was also a door the appetite would love to learn. And he watched it fail to land the way it had landed three times before. For one hour tonight, Satoru had learned that resting and stopping were not the same thing. A man who has felt that difference cannot quite unfeel it.

She did not push. Her kind never pushed. Pushing would show the method, and the method only worked while it looked like nothing but kindness. She simply took in that tonight's bed would go unslept in. She adjusted with that same smooth ease, and folded her hands.
"The room will keep," she said, mild and warm, to him and past him to Rei. "It's no trouble. Everyone needs somewhere to stop, in the end. Even him."

The even him was aimed at Rei. It was small and precise. A note being filed. The ninth seat could be carried through movement by someone with a wall instead of an address. The shaped thing that had walked the river tonight was exactly the kind of tool their work could use. Without meaning to, Rei had shown the other side a tool while he thought he was only saving a man. He had come to keep a holder away from her door. He had also taught the people who were thinning the wall a new way to think about doors. And about him.

When she had gone back inside and the gold light of the screens had closed behind her, Satoru stood in the lane. The festival murmured its way down toward the river. Beyond the rooftops, lanterns were still floating out on the black water.

He was not fixed. He would be moving again before dawn, because the seat was a sentence and Rei had not shortened it. But he stood in the lane like a man who had remembered that there is a difference between a road and a current.
"She'll find another one," he said. "Somebody who hasn't learned the river yet. There's always somebody more tired than they can stand to be."

He was not wrong. Somewhere across the thin ward there was a seat for every want, and a soft voice with a bed or a meal or a kindness shaped exactly to that want. Rei could not walk every river. But he had walked this one.
"Thank you for carrying it," Satoru said.
It was the oddest thanks and the truest. What he meant was thank you for showing me I don't only get to choose between starving and stopping.
Then he was gone, between one step and the next, the way he had crossed the road.

Rei walked home alone along the river. Despair, Rage, Fear, and now Hunger. Four seats, he thought, and every one of them visited by someone soft, and all of it in the same two weeks. A campaign that had been patient for years had suddenly begun to hurry. He wondered what it knew about the calendar that he did not.
